lead: Paul tells Timothy to train himself in godliness as an athlete trains his body, which is a fitting word in a fast. John shows the crowd, the temple police and the authorities divided over Jesus, and one man, Nicodemus, asking only that he be given a fair hearing. Training in godliness begins with this kind of honest listening.

set: The First Letter to Timothy, received by the Church among the letters of St Paul, gives guidance to a young church leader at Ephesus. Just before this passage it warns of teachers who “forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods”, and answers that “everything created by God is good” (4:3–4). So the training Paul now commends is not contempt for the body or for food. Christian fasting does not come from thinking creation is bad.
str: v. 6: the good servant, nourished on sound teaching.
vv. 7–8: leave aside the myths; train in godliness, which is useful for this life and the next.
vv. 9–10: a trustworthy saying, and the reason for the effort: hope in the living God.
kw: From the word for athletic training, which also gives us “gymnasium”. Godliness does not happen by itself; it needs regular practice, as a body does.
A favourite word of these letters: reverence for God lived out in daily conduct. The POC has “ദൈവഭക്തി” in v. 7 and “ആത്മീയത” in v. 8.
A formula found five times in the letters to Timothy and Titus (for example 1 Timothy 1:15), which marks a saying the Church can rely on.
vv: Have nothing to do with profane myths and old wives’ tales. Train yourself in godliness,
The contrast is between speculation that goes nowhere and practice that changes a life.
for, while physical training is of some value, godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for both the present life and the life to come.
Bodily training is not despised: it has “some value”. But its benefits end with this life, while godliness carries over.
For to this end we toil and struggle, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
“Struggle” translates a word used for athletic contests. The effort is not self-improvement: it is hope in a God who wants to save all (compare 1 Timothy 2:4).
ch: “There is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle,” says the Catechism, and spiritual progress requires ascesis and mortification (CCC 2015). The two saints of today lived this in different ways. Mar Saba spent long years in the desert and founded a community of monks there. St Clement of Alexandria wrote a work called The Tutor (Paedagogus), in which Christ is the one who patiently trains Christians in daily conduct.

r.h: Never has anyone spoken like this
set: The scene is the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem (7:2). On its last day Jesus has cried out, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me” (7:37). The crowd is now divided. Some think he is “the prophet” like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15; some, the Messiah; some object that he is from Galilee. Temple police sent earlier to arrest him (7:32) come back without him.

John does not speak here of a whole people rejecting Jesus. He shows a division among ordinary people and among the authorities themselves, and a member of the council who speaks up for him. The Church firmly teaches that the Jewish people as a whole must not be blamed for what happened to Jesus (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
str: vv. 40–44: the crowd divided: prophet, Messiah, or neither?
vv. 45–49: the police return: “Never has anyone spoken like this!” The Pharisees' scorn.
vv. 50–52: Nicodemus asks for a hearing and is mocked.
kw: The word from which “schism” comes. It occurs three times in John, always of people divided over Jesus (7:43; 9:16; 10:19). His word forces a decision.
Attendants who kept order in the Temple under the authorities. They came to arrest him, and his words stopped them.
A harsh word from a few leaders, in scorn of ordinary people who have not studied. John quotes it to show how pride in learning can blind.
vv: Has not the scripture said that the Messiah is descended from David and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?”

The speakers are right about the Scriptures (2 Samuel 7:12; Micah 5:2). John leaves an irony for his Christian readers, who know the stories of Jesus' birth: the objection is mistaken because the speakers do not know who stands before them.
The police answered, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”
Men sent with authority return disarmed by a voice. They offer no argument; they only report what they heard.
“Our law does not judge people without first giving them a hearing to find out what they are doing, does it?”
Nicodemus, who came “by night” (3:2), speaks by day now. Deuteronomy 1:16–17 commands fair hearings. He will appear once more, bringing myrrh and aloes for the burial (19:39).
[[ Then each of them went home,

A note on the text. The NRSV brackets v. 53 because it begins the story of the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11), which is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts of John. The Church receives that passage as inspired Scripture all the same.
ch: The Catechism points to this scene to show that the religious authorities in Jerusalem were not of one mind about Jesus: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were secret disciples, and there was long-standing dissension about him (CCC 595). The objection about Galilee reminds Christians that human knowledge, even of Scripture, needs humility before the living Word.

qa: Did no prophet come from Galilee?

The Pharisees' claim in v. 52 is spoken in anger and is not strictly accurate: 2 Kings 14:25 says the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher, a town in the region later called Galilee. John simply reports the words, and his readers can see how little the argument holds.
rite: Mar Saba (died 532) founded the Great Lavra in the Judean desert, which still has monks today; St John of Damascus, remembered yesterday, lived there. St Clement of Alexandria (died around 215) was an early Christian teacher who took the wisdom of the Greeks seriously and led it to Christ. Between them they show the two sides of the Eastern Christian inheritance: the desert and the school. A fast in the Malankara tradition needs both: self-denial and the hearing of the word.
study: What does regular “training in godliness” look like for me in this fast? Name one daily practice.
Like Nicodemus, have I ever had to ask for a fair hearing for someone others were dismissing? Have I been the one dismissing?
